When something or someone is described as "fair game," it means they are a legitimate and acceptable target — for criticism, jokes, investigation, pursuit, or any kind of action. There is nothing wrong, unfair, or against the rules about going after them. Society's unspoken rules permit it.

Think of it this way: "fair" here means allowed or justified, not just pleasant. And the target — the person, topic, or thing — is the "game." So "fair game" literally means: a target you are allowed to go after.

This idiom was born in the world of hunting.

Centuries ago, hunting was governed by strict laws. Hunters could only hunt certain animals during certain seasons. Animals that were legally permitted to be hunted were called "game," and if they could be hunted within the rules, they were called "fair game." An animal that was out of season or protected by law was not fair game — chasing it would be wrong and illegal.

Over time, people took this idea out of the forest and into everyday life. They started using it to mean: "This is something I am allowed to go after — the rules permit it."
How It Works in Real Life

The idiom is used across many different situations, but the logic is always the same: something or someone can be legitimately targeted, and no one can complain about it being unfair.

1. Criticism and Public Figures

The most common use. When a person voluntarily steps into public life — a politician, a celebrity, a CEO — their public actions become fair game. Anyone can criticize, analyze, or joke about those actions, and the person cannot reasonably object.

"The senator voted for that bill, so his record on the issue is fair game for reporters to question."

"She chose to be a public figure. Her business decisions are fair game."

Notice: the criticism is earned or justified by their public role. It's not random or unfair.

2. Debate and Discussion

A topic that is fair game is one that is open and acceptable to discuss or debate, without it being considered rude, off-limits, or taboo in that setting.

"In this philosophy class, every idea — no matter how controversial — is fair game for debate."

"Once you publish your book, your writing style is fair game for literary critics."

3. Competition and Strategy

In competitions, a fair game move or target is one that the rules of the game allow.

"In chess, leaving your queen unprotected makes it fair game for your opponent to capture."

"That company undercut our prices — it's a tough move, but it's fair game in business."

4. Romantic Pursuit

When someone is single and available, they are sometimes described as fair game — meaning others may pursue them romantically, and there is nothing wrong with doing so.

"He and his girlfriend broke up last month. I heard he's fair game now."

5. Humor and Teasing

Among friends or in comedy, certain people or topics are fair game for jokes — meaning everyone has agreed (directly or by unspoken understanding) that joking about that thing is acceptable.

"In our friend group, our terrible fashion choices in high school are always fair game."
The Key Idea Hidden Inside the Idiom

What makes "fair game" interesting and important is that it always implies a set of rules or boundaries. Something being "fair game" means it falls within those boundaries. The phrase is meaningful precisely because some things are not fair game.

For example:

  • A politician's voting record → fair game (public behavior, open to scrutiny).
  • That same politician's young child → not fair game (private, not a public figure, deserves protection).

Or:

  • A celebrity's movie performances → fair game (that's their public work).
  • That same celebrity's private medical records → not fair game (private life, crossing a line).

This is why the word "fair" matters so much. It signals that the targeting is justified, not just possible. You could attack someone's private life, but it wouldn't be fair. It's only "fair game" when there's a reason — a rule, a social norm, a context — that makes it acceptable.

"Fair game" is a neutral-to-slightly-assertive phrase. It is often used when someone is defending the right to criticize or pursue something, especially when someone else has objected.

"You can't complain that I questioned your logic — when you make an argument in public, it's fair game."

It can also be used more casually and lightly, without any confrontation:

"Leftover cake in the office kitchen is fair game. Help yourself!"

The idiom is usually used in these patterns:

  • "X is fair game." → The most common form.
  • "X is fair game for Y." → Specifies who is doing the targeting and why.
  • "Consider X fair game." → An opinion about what should be allowed.
  • "Declare/make X fair game." → Announce that something is now open to targeting.

Examples:

  • "His past statements are fair game."
  • "Her work is fair game for peer review."
  • "I consider the whole topic fair game for this discussion."
  • "The leaked documents made the company's finances fair game for investigators."
What the Idiom Does NOT Mean

A few things to be careful about:

  • It does not mean something is fun or easy to go after. It only means it is permitted.
  • It does not mean that all methods of going after something are acceptable — just that the target itself is acceptable.
  • It is not the same as "fair play," which refers to behaving honestly and by the rules during a competition. "Fair game" is about whether the target is legitimate; "fair play" is about whether your methods are honest.

ConceptExplanation

"Fair game" means a person, topic, or thing that is a legitimate, acceptable, and justified target — for criticism, humor, pursuit, investigation, or action. The phrase comes from hunting, where it referred to animals that could legally be hunted. Today, it is used figuratively in everyday speech to signal that going after something is within the rules — social, ethical, or otherwise. Its power comes from the contrast: not everything is fair game, and calling something "fair game" is a way of saying "this one is — and no one can fairly object."
